name: Private Eye Cyclops crossword No 485
preamble: Answers to asterisked clues are Pseudo Names published in the Eye over the past year or so. The clues are normal cryptic style and/or a rough idea of what the ‘names’ are supposed to sound like. In the case of answers containing one or more invented words, an anagram of the answer appears in square brackets.

solutions.check: 85 entries verified against the grid image (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping); unclued letters checked against the preamble's list

clue.text: Superman champion “loosened” by Heinz beans ultimately, etc.

indicators.note: something loosened has come apart and can settle into a new order
ultimately means at the very end, so only the closing letter of the word is wanted

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of beans
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tin of Heinz beans claims a superhero as its champion, with the contents spilling out.
explanation.walkthrough: Superman here is not the comic hero but the Übermensch, the ideal higher man of German philosophy.
explanation.definitionFit: The German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche proposed the Übermensch, usually translated Superman, so he is its leading advocate.

clue.text: Pitiful elastic – no good as a Wonderbra

definitions.note: a phrase describing the bra; the answer is the adjective it calls for

indicators.note: elastic material stretches and changes shape, so these letters can be pulled into another form

blocks.note: taken as written
NG is the standard abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: A sad, saggy bit of elastic that fails to do what a Wonderbra promises.
explanation.walkthrough: The NG joins the seven letters of Pitiful before the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A Wonderbra is a push-up bra sold on its lifting effect, so describing something as like one means raising or boosting.

clue.text: Sad Miliband’s last to go – given the boot

indicators.note: last points to the very end of the word, so only its closing letter is meant
a letter told to go is removed and leaves the rest behind

blocks.note: dejected means downcast or sad
the final letter of the Labour leader's surname, the one removed

explanation.surface: A gloomy Ed Miliband, Labour leader in 2012, is pushed out of his post.
explanation.walkthrough: The D at the end of Miliband is the one to drop, and it happens to sit at the front of the synonym for sad.
explanation.definitionFit: To be given the boot is an idiom for being thrown out or expelled, which is what being ejected means.

clue.text: Gradually, doggedly, producing ex-TV commentator’s autobiography?

blocks.note: first meaning: slowly and steadily, one step at a time
second meaning: the title of a memoir by the broadcaster Sir Robin Day

explanation.walkthrough: Sir Robin Day was a famously combative British TV interviewer; his 1975 memoir was called Day by Day.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for steady, persistent progress made a little at a time, and also a book title punning on its author's surname.

clue.text: Rank date by Brenda’s realm and Dome fiasco

indicators.note: a fiasco is a shambles, so these letters end up thoroughly jumbled

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for date
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose realm is the UK
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dig at the Millennium Dome, the costly 2000 flop, and the Queen's kingdom.
explanation.walkthrough: The Millennium Dome was a notorious white elephant in London; here it is just four letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A dukedom is the title and status of a duke, one of the grades of the British peerage.

clue.text: Headline: “Do away with police force!”

blocks.note: to top someone is slang for to kill them
the Bill is British slang for the police

explanation.surface: A newspaper banner calling for the police to be abolished.
explanation.walkthrough: Headline looks like a noun, the banner over a story, but it is the verb: to be the main act.
explanation.definitionFit: To headline a show is to be its star attraction, named first on the poster, which is the idiom's meaning.

clue.text: Carlton’s chief pisspoor ‘Numeric TV’ dodge

indicators.note: the chief part of a word is its head, the opening letter
something pisspoor is a botched job, so the letters come out badly scrambled

blocks.note: the first letter of Carlton
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sneer at Carlton, an ITV company, for a feeble digital TV service, Carlton's ill-fated ONdigital venture.
explanation.walkthrough: Carlton was a London ITV broadcaster whose ONdigital pay-TV service collapsed in 2002.
explanation.definitionFit: To circumvent a rule or obstacle is to find a way around it, so it is a synonym of dodge as a verb.

clue.text: * Benefit from extra shagging, 007-style?

definitions.note: names the actor who played 007 rather than describing a style

blocks.note: surface padding: to benefit from extra sex is to be rogered more, which sets up the pair of words
to roger is British slang for to have sex with
extra means more, spelt here as the surname

explanation.surface: A womaniser getting an extra helping of sex, just like James Bond.
explanation.walkthrough: Benefit from extra shagging is roger more; respelling the second word gives the name. The starred clues mark the puzzle's pseudo names, punning names from Private Eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Roger Moore played James Bond, agent 007, in seven films, so the actor is the original of a Bond style.

clue.text: see 28ac.
*[A Royal highness ham con] a 2012 finale

definitions.note: defines CLOSING CEREMONY; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on names

indicators.note: the star marks one of the puzzle's themed clues, whose bracketed letters must be rearranged to make the entry

blocks.note: every letter in the brackets is used

explanation.surface: A sly suggestion that a royal's appearance at the end of the London Olympics was a bit of hammy fakery.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, Chloe Singh Sarah Moany is closing ceremony, the show that ended the London 2012 Olympics.
explanation.definitionFit: The London Olympic Games of 2012 ended with a closing ceremony, the final spectacle of the event.

clue.text: Eye after, er, overturning Inquiry

indicators.note: turning something over puts its end at the front
after says which piece follows, so the earlier-printed word goes second

blocks.note: taken as written
to eye something is to view it

explanation.surface: Private Eye, hesitating, after an official inquiry finds against it.
explanation.walkthrough: Eye is the verb, to look at, not the magazine; it comes after the turned two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A review is a formal examination of something, such as a public inquiry into a policy or event.

clue.text: Sock-hoisting advice ill-advised for a wanker?

blocks.note: first meaning: the urging to pull your socks up, to buck up
second meaning: the same words taken literally, the last thing a masturbator needs telling

explanation.walkthrough: Pull your socks up is a British idiom for try harder; the phrase meaning the same thing becomes rude when taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling someone to pull their socks up and to get a grip are both idioms urging them to regain control of themselves.

clue.text: Rocks ache on receiving Fergie’s ‘premier’ rub

indicators.note: a thing that rocks is shaken about, so its letters are jolted out of order
to receive is to take in, so one piece goes inside another
premier means first, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of Fergie

explanation.surface: Sir Alex Ferguson, Manchester United's manager, as the source of an aching rub to the rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: Rocks looks like the subject of the sentence, a noun, but it is a verb telling you to shake up ache.
explanation.definitionFit: To chafe is to wear or irritate by rubbing, so it works as a verb synonym of rub.

clue.text: Chief characters in expenses disgrace securing next grotesque increase

indicators.note: the chief characters of words are their opening letters
securing something means holding it fast, so these letters enclose the rest
something grotesque is distorted out of its normal shape

blocks.note: the first letter of expenses
taken as written
the first letter of disgrace

explanation.surface: The MPs' expenses scandal of 2009, with a further outrageous pay rise on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The two opening letters wrap round the rearranged four, rather than sitting side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To extend something is to make it longer or larger, so it serves as a verb synonym of increase.

clue.text: Savile-preferred customised dungaree?

indicators.note: a customised item has been altered and remade to a new design

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fashion note about a celebrity's taste in tailored dungarees.
explanation.walkthrough: Jimmy Savile was a BBC presenter exposed after his death in 2011 as a prolific child abuser.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is a grim joke: Savile's victims were largely children, below the legal age of consent.

clue.text: Green ballsed up, letting in elected representative at last for Telford?

definitions.note: an example of the answer, as the question mark admits

indicators.note: something ballsed up has been botched and left in a mess
to let something in is to admit it inside, so one piece goes within another
at last points to the very end, so only the closing letter counts

blocks.note: taken as written
someone elected is in office
the final letter of representative

explanation.surface: A Green politician fluffs it while letting in an elected representative for Telford, a Shropshire constituency.
explanation.walkthrough: Telford looks like a parliamentary seat, a town in Shropshire, but it is Thomas Telford, the Scottish builder of roads, bridges and canals.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Telford designed the Menai Bridge and many canals, so he is a celebrated example of a civil engineer.

clue.text: Nuts central on getting screwed, that’s clear

indicators.note: a screw twists round, so these letters are turned into a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A workshop picture of nuts screwed onto a central bolt, with a satisfied verdict.
explanation.walkthrough: Nuts and screwed both suggest hardware, but nuts is just fodder and screwed the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Translucent material lets light pass through, so it is loosely clear, though not fully see-through.

clue.text: see 63ac.
Basking in warm glow of books aimed at tabloid readers?

blocks.note: the Sun is Britain's best-selling tabloid newspaper
lit is short for literature

explanation.surface: Someone glowing contentedly over a pile of books written for the mass-market tabloid reader.
explanation.walkthrough: Sun lit would be literature for readers of the Sun, Rupert Murdoch's British red-top paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sunlit is lit by the sun, so it is bathed in a warm natural light.

clue.text: Balls and Straw back, which is rough

definitions.note: a noun here: a rough, a rowdy lout

indicators.note: going back means running from the end towards the start

blocks.note: two round shapes look like a pair of O's
hay is dried grass, much like straw

explanation.surface: Ed Balls and Jack Straw, Labour heavyweights, making a political comeback that is going roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: Balls and Straw look like the politicians Ed Balls and Jack Straw, but each is a plain word supplying letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A yahoo is a coarse, loutish person, from Swift's brutish creatures, and a rough is a hooligan, so both are noun synonyms.

clue.text: “Firm” Alan on TV is pointless, catty thing

indicators.note: the points of the compass are N, E, S and W, so a word without a point loses one of those letters

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
Alan Sugar is the businessman who hosts the British version of The Apprentice

explanation.surface: A jibe at Lord Sugar on television, calling him spiteful and futile.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass point dropped is the S at the front of the TV tycoon's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A cougar is a large American wild cat, the puma, so it is literally a feline creature; catty plays on spitefulness.

clue.text: Smear: Blair’s leading pair trashed

blocks.note: a blot is a smear or stain
the opening two letters of Tony, Blair's first name

explanation.surface: A smear campaign leaves Tony Blair and his deputy's reputations wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: The two letters come from the former Prime Minister's first name, Tony, not from the printed surname. Trashed is slang for very drunk, not wrecked.
explanation.definitionFit: Blotto is British slang for extremely drunk, and trashed is another slang word for the same helpless state.

clue.text: A spent nation‘s fat broadcast

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard over the air, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: grease is fat used in cooking

explanation.surface: A bankrupt country's fat salaries announced on the news.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2012 Greece was at the centre of the eurozone debt crisis, needing repeated bailouts, hence spent.
explanation.definitionFit: Greece is a nation that had run out of money by 2012, so a spent nation is a topical description of it.

clue.text: Shabby ‘bum fluff’ by arse

blocks.note: bum fluff is British slang for a youth's first wispy beard, soft down
by and at both mean located next to
an arse is a contemptible person, as is a heel

explanation.surface: A scruffy youth's attempt at a beard, summed up rudely.
explanation.walkthrough: Bum fluff is the downy hair on a teenage boy's chin, nothing to do with a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Down at heel describes worn shoes and so, by extension, a shabby, run-down appearance.

clue.text: Roger’s tackle?

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, vulgar slang for to have sex with
second meaning: a noun, gear or equipment

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a man named Roger and his tackle, slang for genitals; really both words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To roger is to have sex with, crudely to stuff someone, and fishing tackle is gear, one's stuff.

clue.text: I do fantastically, wearing Goldsmith junior’s heavenly belt

indicators.note: fantastically means in a wild, fanciful way, so the letters are freely reshaped
to be worn is to be enclosed by clothes, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
Zac Goldsmith, Tory MP, is the son of the tycoon Sir James Goldsmith

explanation.surface: Someone boasting of looking great in a belt that belongs to the young Goldsmith.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged three letters go inside the MP's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The zodiac is the band of sky through which the sun, moon and planets move, a celestial belt.

clue.text: Blow job material, put coarsely, these

definitions.text: Blow job material, put coarsely, these

blocks.note: surface reading: something to do with oral sex
setter's reading: crude slang for what you use when you blow your nose

explanation.walkthrough: The blowing here is of the nose; the coarse phrase is a slangy name for handkerchiefs.
explanation.definitionFit: Handkerchiefs are cloths for blowing your nose into, and this phrase is a vulgar British term for them.

clue.text: Canon in less unseemly description of bollocks

indicators.note: unseemly behaviour is improper and disorderly, so these letters are out of their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A clergyman trying to describe rubbish in a less vulgar way.
explanation.walkthrough: Bollocks here is the British slang for nonsense, rather than the anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bollocks is British slang for rubbish talk, and nonsensical is the adjective you would apply to it.

clue.text: * Toff leader’s name on list, say, for old sexy story collection

definitions.note: defines THE DECAMERON; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on a name

indicators.note: say means as it is spoken, so the sound decides and not the spelling

blocks.note: Etonian Tory leader David Cameron, as he would be listed with his initial

explanation.surface: The posh Prime Minister's name in a register, oddly linked to a classic book of bawdy tales.
explanation.walkthrough: The starred clues are pseudo names; written as initial and surname, the Prime Minister's name sounds like Boccaccio's book. A toff is a posh person.
explanation.definitionFit: Boccaccio's Decameron is a fourteenth-century Italian collection of a hundred tales, many of them bawdy.

clue.text: * French weightlifter’s cry?

definitions.note: defines HEAVE-HO; the entry respells it in French

blocks.note: the lifter's call as a French speaker says it, dropping both H sounds, and spelt with the French name Yves and the French word eaux

explanation.surface: A French strongman grunting as he heaves a barbell overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: Heave-ho without the H sounds like eve-oh, spelt with a French man's name and the French for waters.
explanation.definitionFit: Heave-ho is the traditional shout given when hauling or lifting something heavy together.

clue.text: Oracle’s place, specialist shop welcoming the boozer

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a deli sells specialist foods
a boozer is a pub, a public house, abbreviated PH

explanation.surface: An upmarket food shop that lets the local drunk in.
explanation.walkthrough: Boozer looks like a heavy drinker but is British slang for a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Delphi in ancient Greece was the seat of the most famous oracle, the priestess of Apollo.

clue.text: Broadcaster second rate? “Heavens, Brucie’s no. 1!”

indicators.note: number one is the first in line, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: a B grade is second rate
the heavens are the sky
the first letter of Brucie

explanation.surface: A sneer at a second-rate broadcaster, with an exclamation about Bruce Forsyth, the veteran TV host, being top.
explanation.walkthrough: Brucie is the British game-show host Sir Bruce Forsyth; only his initial is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: BSkyB, British Sky Broadcasting, was the Murdoch-backed satellite television company, so it is literally a broadcaster.

clue.text: * In vain, bestowing biblical name on dell

definitions.note: defines TO NO AVAIL; the entry is a punning respelling built on a name

blocks.note: Noah built the ark in Genesis
a dell and a vale are both small valleys

explanation.surface: A futile attempt to give a little valley a name from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, Noah Vale is no avail, as in the phrase to no avail.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done to no avail is done uselessly, without result, which is what in vain means.

clue.text: Elisabeth: “Nice protecting a racial sort”

definitions.note: ethnic as a noun, a member of an ethnic minority

indicators.note: something protected is held safely inside, so the letters are kept within the words

blocks.note: runs across the end of the name and the start of the town

explanation.surface: A woman called Elisabeth vouching that Nice, on the French Riviera, shelters someone of a particular race.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice looks like an adjective but is the French city; its first three letters finish the run.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, an ethnic is a person belonging to a racial or cultural minority group, a dated usage.

clue.text: Recession: PM bins Helen’s interpretation as gobbledegook

indicators.note: an interpretation is a reworking of the original into a different version

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister throws out an adviser's baffling account of the economic downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of the four words is used, all twenty; only the apostrophe-s on Helen is left over.
explanation.definitionFit: Gobbledegook is meaningless jargon, and incomprehensibleness is the quality of being impossible to understand.

clue.text: Russell Brand type shagger’s game?

blocks.note: Russell Brand, the comedian, is a self-styled womaniser, a stud
to poke is slang for to have sex with, so a shagger is a poker

explanation.surface: Russell Brand, famous for bedding women, and the sport he plays.
explanation.walkthrough: Game looks like the womaniser's sport of seduction; it is the card game.
explanation.definitionFit: Stud poker is a variety of poker in which some cards are dealt face up, a card game.

clue.text: * [Yon Liberal] who’s loaded

definitions.note: defines BILLIONAIRE; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on a name

indicators.note: the star marks one of the puzzle's themed clues, whose bracketed letters must be rearranged to make the entry

blocks.note: every letter in the brackets is used

explanation.surface: Pointing at a Liberal over there who is very rich.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Onare sounds like billionaire, with the first name Billy worked in.
explanation.definitionFit: A billionaire has a fortune of at least a thousand million, and loaded is slang for very rich.

clue.text: A particular gear, spicy, wrapped round Eva’s top – a Hitler creation

indicators.note: the top of a word is its head, the first letter
to wrap round something is to enclose it

blocks.note: third gear on a car
rich food is highly flavoured
the first letter of Eva

explanation.surface: Eva Braun dressed in a racy outfit for Hitler.
explanation.walkthrough: Eva is Eva Braun, Hitler's companion, but only her initial is used; spicy means rich, as in racy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Third Reich was the name Hitler's Nazi regime gave to Germany from 1933 to 1945.

clue.text: Screwed, cruising around the state – topping!

indicators.note: something screwed up is twisted out of shape
to go around something is to enclose it

blocks.note: taken as written
GA is the abbreviation for Georgia, a US state

explanation.surface: A drunk driving round a US state, cheering a terrific trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Topping is the noun, something put on a cake, not the British exclamation for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Icing sugar is finely powdered sugar used to make cake icing or dusted on top of desserts.

clue.text: Fast mover, not the faithful type by the sound of it

indicators.note: the phrase asks you to judge by what you hear, not what is written

blocks.note: an unfaithful partner is a cheater

explanation.surface: A fast worker, romantically speaking, who sounds unreliable.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech the final R of cheater is silent, so it sounds like the cat. A fast mover is also slang for a quick seducer.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheetah is the fastest land animal, reaching about seventy miles an hour in short bursts.

clue.text: Smart arse scruffy teens, taking Cyclops in

indicators.note: scruffy means untidy, so the letters are messed about

blocks.note: taken as written
the setter refers to himself, so Cyclops is I
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clever-clogs gang of messy teenagers letting the crossword setter join them.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's own pseudonym gives the I that joins the five letters before they are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone an Einstein is a sarcastic way to label a know-all, after the famous physicist's genius.

clue.text: No oral sex available – proceed somewhere else

blocks.note: first meaning: head is slang for oral sex, and off means not on offer, as a dish is off the menu
second meaning: to set out or depart

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is the setter's crude joke, a menu note that one service is off.
explanation.definitionFit: To head off is an everyday idiom for leaving or setting out in some direction.

clue.text: Andy right pissed – adding water!

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of line

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Andy thoroughly drunk and being told to drink water.
explanation.walkthrough: Pissed is British slang for drunk, not American for angry.
explanation.definitionFit: To hydrate something is to supply it with water, so hydrating means adding water.

clue.text: Positive types‘ yen: easy arse movement

indicators.note: a movement shifts things from where they were

blocks.note: Y is the abbreviation for the Japanese yen
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Upbeat people with a longing for an easy bowel movement.
explanation.walkthrough: Yen looks like a longing but is the Japanese currency, giving one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Yea-sayers are people who habitually agree or say yes, so they are positive types.

clue.text: A national air display attended by Queen and Cyclops

indicators.note: a display puts things on show in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
Q is the abbreviation for queen, as in chess notation
the setter refers to himself, so Cyclops is I

explanation.surface: A national air show attended by the Queen and the crossword setter.
explanation.walkthrough: A national is a noun, a citizen of some country, not an adjective attached to the air display.
explanation.definitionFit: An Iraqi is a citizen of Iraq, so a national of that country.

clue.text: Snout inside, stuck in pipe?

blocks.note: first meaning: in British prison slang snout is smoking material, and inside means in jail
second meaning: what a smoker packs into a pipe

explanation.walkthrough: Snout looks like a nose stuck in a pipe; in British prison slang it is tobacco, and inside means in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobacco is the currency of prison life, called snout by inmates, and it is what is smoked in a pipe.

clue.text: Put another way, M&S exhibiting strongly opposing sexual tendencies?

definitions.note: M&S turned round is S&M, the abbreviation, an adjective here as in S&M gear

blocks.note: first meaning: the initials of the store Marks & Spencer swapped round give the sexual abbreviation S&M
second meaning: enjoying both inflicting and receiving pain

explanation.surface: Marks & Spencer, the staid British store, accused of kinky sexual leanings.
explanation.walkthrough: M&S is Marks & Spencer, a byword for respectable British shopping; turned round it reads S&M, short for the answer's practice.
explanation.definitionFit: The word combines sadism and masochism, enjoying giving pain and enjoying receiving it, two opposed sexual tastes.

clue.text: *[Hey, lay Kelly? Na’], not much chance of that

definitions.note: defines HIGHLY UNLIKELY; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on names

indicators.note: the star marks one of the puzzle's themed clues, whose bracketed letters must be rearranged to make the entry

blocks.note: every letter in the brackets is used

explanation.surface: A man asks if he might sleep with Kelly and is turned down flat.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, Hayley N Lakely is highly unlikely, with the first name Hayley worked in.
explanation.definitionFit: Highly unlikely means very improbable, which is what not much chance of that says in conversation.

clue.text: see 70ac.
Hot dating collapsed without nitrogen – pissed off

indicators.note: something collapsed has fallen apart and lies in a heap
without in its old sense means outside, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: hot and in both mean fashionable
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Without looks like lacking, but here it means outside: the jumbled six letters go round the chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Indignant means angry at unfair treatment, and pissed off is British slang for annoyed.

clue.text: Watch Merkel’s top during row

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter
something happening during another sits within it

blocks.note: the first letter of Merkel
a tier is a row of seats

explanation.surface: Angela Merkel, the German Chancellor, keeps an eye on her top during a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: Row looks like a quarrel but is a line of seats, a tier.
explanation.definitionFit: A watch is a timepiece and a timer is a device that measures time, so both measure passing minutes.

clue.text: Speculative, in no way a lion, ballsed up

indicators.note: something ballsed up has been botched and left in a mess

blocks.note: not means in no way
taken as written

explanation.surface: A guess that someone is no lion, made a mess of.
explanation.walkthrough: Ballsed up is British slang for botched.
explanation.definitionFit: Notional means existing only in theory or as an idea, so it is a synonym of speculative or hypothetical.

clue.text: see 73dn.
One who’d give way when ‘stupid bird’ squeezes in? Not this road-user!

indicators.note: something stupid makes no sense, so these letters are muddled
to squeeze in is to force oneself inside, so one piece ends up within another

blocks.note: one who caves in gives way
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cautious driver letting a dim woman cut in, unlike a certain kind of motorist.
explanation.walkthrough: Give way sounds like the road sign, but here it means yield or cave in. Not this ends the clue with a joke that taxi drivers never give way.
explanation.definitionFit: A cab driver spends the working day on the roads, so is a professional road-user.

clue.text: Two bodies lined up, energy doubled eating prunes

indicators.note: something eaten ends up inside the eater

blocks.note: E is the symbol for energy, written twice
to prune a hedge is to clip it

explanation.surface: Two people in a queue, full of energy after eating prunes.
explanation.walkthrough: Prunes looks like dried plums, the laxative joke, but it is the verb, as in pruning a hedge.
explanation.definitionFit: An eclipse happens when the sun, moon and earth line up so one celestial body blocks another.

clue.text: Dump Dave’s principal fancy

indicators.note: the principal letter of a word is its first, the one at the head

blocks.note: the first letter of Dave
an itch is a craving or fancy

explanation.surface: David Cameron's main whim is to dump something.
explanation.walkthrough: Dave is David Cameron, Prime Minister in 2012, but only his initial is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To ditch something is to get rid of it, so it works as a verb synonym of dump.

clue.text: * Turned into a victim, [cry “cut deep!”]

definitions.note: defines PERSECUTED; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on a name

indicators.note: the star marks one of the puzzle's themed clues, whose bracketed letters must be rearranged to make the entry

blocks.note: every letter in the brackets is used

explanation.surface: Someone made a victim, wailing that the wound is deep.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, Percy Cuted is persecuted, with the name Percy worked in.
explanation.definitionFit: To be persecuted is to be hounded and harassed, made the victim of sustained ill-treatment.

clue.text: Irresponsible direct bank loans?

indicators.note: irresponsible conduct is wild and disorderly, so the letters are thrown about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dig at reckless lending by banks dealing directly with customers, as in the run-up to the 2008 crash.
explanation.walkthrough: Irresponsible looks like a comment on banking but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Credit is money lent by banks to be repaid later, so it is a collective term for their loans.

clue.text: see 48ac.
Tug on Anne’s bust as a grammatical activist

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so its letters come apart

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone pulls at Princess Anne's bosom, posing as a pedantic campaigner.
explanation.walkthrough: Bust looks like a bosom but is the signal for breaking up the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent noun names the doer of an action, like worker or campaigner, so it is grammar's word for an active person.

clue.text: A sign of the origins of Murdoch’s insidiously perverted tabloid

indicators.note: origins are beginnings, so the opening letters of words are wanted
to pervert is literally to turn the wrong way round

blocks.note: the first letter of Murdoch
the first letter of insidiously
the Sun is Rupert Murdoch's British tabloid

explanation.surface: A sign that Rupert Murdoch's paper has been corrupted by sinister methods, as in the phone-hacking scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: Perverted looks like moral corruption but in its root sense means turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Minus is the mathematical sign for subtraction, a short horizontal line.

clue.text: Revocation of cavorting nun in mental anguish

indicators.note: cavorting means leaping about, so the letters jump out of place
in places one piece inside another
anguish is torment, and tormented letters are twisted out of shape

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A nun dancing about in torment, with something being revoked.
explanation.walkthrough: Mental anguish reads as one phrase, but mental is fodder and anguish its anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An annulment is the formal cancelling of something, such as a marriage, so it is a revocation.

clue.text: Dirty digger – heart-breaking stirrer

indicators.note: something breaking falls into pieces that can be reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written
something that stirs is a mover

explanation.surface: A sleazy gold-digger who breaks hearts and causes trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Dirty digger sounds like a sleazy gold-digger; it is a bulldozer, dirty from shifting soil.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthmover is a heavy machine such as a bulldozer or excavator, which digs and shifts soil.

clue.text: Controversial MP “let in homosexual”

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: gay means homosexual
to let is to allow

explanation.surface: A quote from a divisive MP campaigning to admit gay people.
explanation.walkthrough: Let in reads as a phrase, but let gives the inner piece and in places it.
explanation.definitionFit: George Galloway, Respect MP for Bradford West in 2012, is famously controversial, from Saddam to Celebrity Big Brother.

clue.text: Stroke one applied to two mates with erection for regular beat

indicators.note: something erected stands up, and in a down clue going up turns the letters round

blocks.note: to stroke is to rub
a means one
bud is American slang for a friend, written twice

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of stroking with a pair of friends, keeping a steady rhythm.
explanation.walkthrough: Erection is the reversal signal, since this is a down clue and the letters read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Rub-a-dub-dub imitates the steady sound of a drum, as in the nursery rhyme, so it suggests a regular beat.

clue.text: Eye’s seized by government agency, all over being ‘Spartan’

definitions.note: the answer used as an adjective

indicators.note: something seized is held inside a grip
turned all over means flipped end to end

blocks.note: the CIA is the US Central Intelligence Agency
a private eye is a detective, a tec, plus the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: Private Eye is raided by a state agency and comes out looking austere.
explanation.walkthrough: Eye looks like the magazine but is a private eye, a detective; the detective's letters sit inside the agency before the whole is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Spartan means austere and self-denying, like the ancient Spartans, and an ascetic lifestyle avoids comfort and luxury.

clue.text: Defeated in the House, very old Heath gets depressed?

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for very
O is the abbreviation for old
Sir Edward Heath, Tory Prime Minister 1970 to 1974, was known as Ted
down means depressed

explanation.surface: Ted Heath, the elderly former Prime Minister, losing a Commons vote and feeling low.
explanation.walkthrough: Heath looks like heathland but is the former Prime Minister, whose first name supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A motion voted down in the House of Commons has been rejected by a majority, defeated in Parliament.

clue.text: Great teller of stories, Putin at heart, getting press onto the state

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so the middle letter is wanted

blocks.note: the middle letter of Putin
to press someone is to urge them
Nev is an abbreviation for Nevada, a US state

explanation.surface: A Russian storyteller and Vladimir Putin, leaning on the state press.
explanation.walkthrough: Putin and the press suggest Russian media; it is a Russian writer, but built from small pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan Turgenev was a nineteenth-century Russian novelist and short-story writer, author of Fathers and Sons.

clue.text: ‘Altruistic‘ Sun is smitten – “Gnome is hot!”

indicators.note: smitten literally means struck, and struck letters are knocked about

blocks.note: taken as written
a gnome and an elf are both little folk of legend
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: The Sun newspaper swooning over Lord Gnome, Private Eye's mythical proprietor, as selfless.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Gnome is Private Eye's fictional owner; here gnome is just a small mythical being.
explanation.definitionFit: Altruistic means acting for the good of others, which is what being unselfish means.

clue.text: * Woman and two men from same family? They’re of great interest, architecturally

definitions.note: defines LISTED BUILDINGS; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on names

blocks.note: Liz is a woman's name
Ted and Bill are two men's names
the shared surname of all three

explanation.surface: A family of three, one woman and two men, fascinating to architecture lovers.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, Liz Ted Bill Dings is listed buildings. In Britain a listed building is one protected by law for its architectural or historic value.
explanation.definitionFit: Listed buildings are put on an official register because of their special architectural or historic interest.

clue.text: * Butler’s candid preface to his famous classic film quote [irked rifleman]

definitions.text: Butler’s candid preface to his famous classic film quote
definitions.note: defines FRANKLY MY DEAR; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on a name

indicators.note: the star marks one of the puzzle's themed clues, whose bracketed letters must be rearranged to make the entry

blocks.note: every letter in the brackets is used

explanation.surface: A butler's honest opening words, set against an annoyed soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: Butler is Rhett Butler in Gone with the Wind, whose famous line begins with these words; Frank is a name and also means candid.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhett Butler's parting line is Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn, so these words open it.

clue.text: Bland peacekeepers withdrawing (China’s first to enter)

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter
to enter is to go inside, so one piece is put within another

blocks.note: the United Nations sends peacekeeping forces
exiting means leaving or withdrawing
the first letter of China

explanation.surface: A dull news item about UN peacekeepers pulling out while China moves in.
explanation.walkthrough: The single letter goes inside the word for withdrawing, which then follows the two-letter peacekeepers.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bland is dull and lacking flavour or interest, which is what unexciting means.

clue.text: Greek character with money matters, less means of keeping on even keel, makes subtle difference

definitions.note: the answer as a verb, to nuance

indicators.note: less is the arithmetic minus sign, so some letters are subtracted

blocks.note: nu is the thirteenth letter of the Greek alphabet
finance is the management of money

blocks.clueFragment: means of keeping on even keel
blocks.note: a fin keeps a boat or fish stable, the part removed

explanation.surface: A Greek dealing with money and trying to keep things steady, in the debt crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: Even keel suggests calm finances, but the means of keeping on it is a stabilising fin.
explanation.definitionFit: To nuance something is to give it shades of meaning, so it introduces slight distinctions.

clue.text: Cook Nigella’s butt in stock

indicators.note: a butt is the thick end of something, so only the last letter is wanted
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: the last letter of Nigella
a stock is a stem or trunk of a plant

explanation.surface: Nigella Lawson, the TV cook, with her famous curves dipped in stock.
explanation.walkthrough: Cook looks like the job title before Nigella, but it is the verb defining the answer; stock is the plant stem, not soup.
explanation.definitionFit: To steam food is to cook it in the vapour of boiling water, a standard cooking method.

clue.text: see 53ac.
Brown‘s star went up in flames

blocks.note: the sun is a star
burned means went up in flames

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown, the former Prime Minister, whose rising star crashed and burned.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown looks like Gordon Brown but is the colour of skin after too much sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunburned skin is reddened or tanned by the sun, so in a loose sense it is brown.

clue.text: “Unremoveable MP” is turned with a tenner

indicators.note: something turned is twisted into a new shape

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An MP with a safe seat bribed with a ten-pound note.
explanation.walkthrough: A tenner is British slang for a ten-pound note; here it is just seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Permanent means lasting indefinitely, so something permanent cannot be removed or ended.

clue.text: Comically topless in an Eye-related way

indicators.note: topless means with the top removed, which in a down clue is the first letter

blocks.note: jocularly means in a joking way

explanation.surface: Private Eye's lurid way of being funny about topless models.
explanation.walkthrough: Eye is capitalised to suggest the magazine; ocular simply means to do with the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocular means relating to the eyes, so the adverb describes doing something by means of the eye.

clue.text: * Hardy sister of Sebastian establishes store?

definitions.note: defines TESCO; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on names

blocks.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles is Thomas Hardy's best-known heroine
a sister of the athlete Sebastian Coe would share his surname

explanation.surface: A tough female relation of Sebastian Coe, head of the London 2012 Olympics, opening a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy looks like the adjective tough, but it is the novelist Thomas Hardy. Said aloud the name is Tesco, Britain's biggest supermarket chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Tesco is the largest supermarket chain in Britain, so it is an obvious example of a store.

clue.text: Evidence of having scored, weight lifted with chain?

indicators.note: lifting in a down clue sends the letters upwards, so they read backwards

blocks.note: a ton is a unit of weight
CH is the abbreviation for chain, an old unit of length

explanation.surface: A weightlifter with a chain showing off a sexual conquest.
explanation.walkthrough: Scored here means had sex; a womaniser is said to cut a notch on his bedpost for each conquest.
explanation.definitionFit: A notch cut in a bedpost or stick is the traditional tally mark recording a conquest or score.

clue.text: New Tory constitution embracing ‘two ways’, hardly a way to get in

definitions.text: hardly a way to get in

indicators.note: a constitution is how something is made up, so the letters are made up afresh
to embrace is to hold in one's arms, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
taken as written
east and north are two directions, compass ways

explanation.surface: A new Conservative party charter that is two-faced and shuts outsiders out.
explanation.walkthrough: Constitution looks like a party rulebook, but it is the signal to rearrange Tory.
explanation.definitionFit: A No Entry sign forbids going in, so it marks a way you cannot get in by.

clue.text: O for a policeman‘s prize figure?

blocks.note: first meaning: the code word for the letter O in the radio alphabet used by police
second meaning: the statuette awarded at the Academy Awards

explanation.walkthrough: The police radio alphabet runs Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, and so on; its word for O is the name of the film award.
explanation.definitionFit: The phonetic alphabet word for O is also the golden statuette given to Academy Award winners.

clue.text: Pop star Jack: “No hotel to be trashed before noon”

indicators.note: something trashed is wrecked and its parts scattered

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: A rock star's rule that no hotel room gets wrecked before midday.
explanation.walkthrough: Trashing hotel rooms is the rock-star cliché the surface plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Elton John is one of the best-selling British pop singers of all time, so he is a pop star.

clue.text: Gazzer famously one to tell the whole town?

definitions.text: one to tell the whole town

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who weeps, as Gazza did

blocks.clueFragment: one to tell the whole town
blocks.note: second meaning: an official who once called out public news in the streets

explanation.walkthrough: Gazza is Paul Gascoigne, the England footballer who famously wept on the pitch at the 1990 World Cup.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who weeps is a crier, and a town crier was an official who shouted announcements in the streets.

clue.text: * What do you take me for? Answer: female going round overturning lives

definitions.text: What do you take me for?

indicators.note: going round means turning to face the other way
overturning something upends it so the order flips

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
F is the abbreviation for female
to live is to exist, as is to be

explanation.surface: An indignant retort followed by a story of a woman turning lives upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: The starred clue gives a pseudo name, Asif, a common first name; lives is the verb, so it means is.
explanation.definitionFit: As if! is a scornful exclamation meaning you must be joking, much like what do you take me for?
